title: Test retention within the current boot before suspecting a reboot problem
explanation: `logger -t telemetryd 'probe'` immediately followed by `journalctl -t telemetryd` shows nothing — not even the line just sent, seconds ago, in this exact boot. That's a meaningfully different symptom from logs merely failing to survive a reboot; it rules out the usual persistence story entirely and points at journald not retaining anything at all, right now.

title: Check the merged config rather than guessing from memory
explanation: `systemd-analyze cat-config systemd/journald.conf` shows a drop-in setting `Storage=none`. It's tempting to assume `Storage=` is just a memory-vs-disk switch, but it isn't.

title: `Storage=` has four distinct modes, and `none` is the one that discards everything
explanation: `persistent` always writes to `/var/log/journal`; `volatile` keeps an in-memory journal under `/run/log/journal` that's queryable for the current boot and lost on reboot; `auto` (the default) is persistent if `/var/log/journal` exists and volatile otherwise. `none` is different in kind, not degree: journald accepts messages and can still forward them elsewhere (syslog, kmsg, console) if configured to, but retains zero history itself — there is nothing for `journalctl` to ever show, even one second after a message was sent.

title: Recognize it as a legitimate setting applied to the wrong box
explanation: `Storage=none` is a real, sensible choice for something like a minimal container image that forwards everything to an external collector and wants zero local disk/memory footprint. Here, though, `telemetryd`'s messages are expected to be queryable locally via `journalctl`, so the setting is simply wrong for what this box actually needs — not misconfigured syntax, a misapplied choice.

title: Switch to a mode that actually retains something, then restart
explanation: `sudo sed -i 's/Storage=none/Storage=auto/' /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/nostore.conf` followed by `sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald` moves journald to a mode that keeps at least an in-memory journal for the current boot.

title: Verify with the same immediate round-trip that first exposed the bug
explanation: `logger -t telemetryd 'confirm'` followed immediately by `journalctl -t telemetryd` now shows the line — the same test from step 1, now succeeding, confirming retention rather than just forwarding is fixed.
